Creating and Updating Figures

Source: vignettes/articles/r-docs/creating-and-updating-figures.Rmd
creating-and-updating-figures.Rmd

The plotly.core R package exists to create, manipulate and render graphical figures (i.e. charts, plots, maps and diagrams) represented by data structures also referred to as figures. The rendering process uses the Plotly.js JavaScript library under the hood although R developers using this package very rarely need to interact with the Javascript library directly, if ever. Figures can be represented in R either as lists or as go_figure() objects, and are serialized as text in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) before being passed to Plotly.js.

Figures As Lists

Figures can be represented as plain R lists and passed to go_figure(), which validates them and returns a figure that can be displayed. The fig list in the example below describes a figure. It contains a single bar trace and a title.

library(plotly.core)
fig = list(
  data = list(
    list(
      x = c(1, 2, 3),
      y = c(1, 3, 2),
      type = 'bar'
    )
  ),
  layout = list(
    title = 'A Figure Specified By R List',
    plot_bgcolor = '#e5ecf6',
    xaxis = list(zerolinecolor = '#ffff', zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = '#ffff'),
    yaxis = list(zerolinecolor = '#ffff', zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = '#ffff')
  )
)
# To display the figure defined by this list, pass it to go_figure()
go_figure(fig)

Graph Objects

The go_*() functions (go_figure(), go_bar(), go_bar_marker(), go_layout(), go_xaxis(), …) provide an automatically-generated hierarchy of classes that may be used to represent figures.

Graph objects have several benefits compared to plain R lists.

  1. Graph objects provide precise data validation. If you provide an invalid property name or an invalid property value, an error will be raised with a helpful message describing the problem.
  2. Graph objects contain descriptions of each valid property in their R documentation. You can use the help pages (e.g. ?go_bar) to learn about the available properties as an alternative to consulting the online Full Reference.
  3. Properties of graph objects can be accessed using list-style lookup (e.g. fig$data[[1]]$x).
  4. Figures support higher-level convenience functions for making updates to already constructed figures (update_layout(), add_trace(), update_traces(), etc).
  5. Figures can be displayed directly, saved as HTML with write_html() and exported as static images with save_image().

Below you can find an example of one way that the figure in the example above could be specified using graph objects instead of a list.

library(plotly.core)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_bar(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(1, 3, 2)) |>
  update_layout(
    title = "A Plotly Figure",
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff"),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff")
  )
fig

Converting Figures To Lists and JSON

A go_figure() is an R list with data, layout and frames elements. You can also retrieve the JSON string representation of a figure using plotly_json().

library(plotly.core)
fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_bar(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(1, 3, 2))
jfig <- plotly_json(fig, jsonedit = FALSE)

cat("List Representation of a figure:")
## List Representation of a figure:
str(unclass(fig), max.level = 2)
## List of 3
##  $ data  :List of 1
##   ..$ :List of 3
##   .. ..- attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "go_bar" "plotly_obj"
##  $ layout: Named list()
##   ..- attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "go_layout" "plotly_obj"
##  $ frames: list()
cat("JSON Representation of a figure:", jfig, sep = "\n\n")
## JSON Representation of a figure:
## 
## {
##   "data": [
##     {
##       "type": "bar",
##       "x": [1,2,3],
##       "y": [1,3,2]
##     }
##   ],
##   "layout": {
##     "template": {
##       "layout": {
##         "margin": {
##           "b": 40,
##           "l": 60,
##           "t": 25,
##           "r": 10
##         }
##       }
##     }
##   },
##   "frames": [],
##   "config": {}
## }

Representing Figures in Dash

Dash for R is an open-source framework for building analytical applications, with no Javascript required, and it is tightly integrated with the Plotly graphing library.

Learn about how to install Dash for R at https://dashr.plot.ly/installation.

Everywhere in this page that you see fig, you can display the same figure in a Dash for R application by passing it to the figure argument.

library(dash)
library(dashCoreComponents)
library(dashHtmlComponents)
library(plotly.core)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_scatter(x = c("a", "b", "c"), y = c(1, 3, 2), mode = "lines") |>
  update_layout(title = "sample figure")

app <- Dash$new()

app$layout(
  htmlDiv(
    list(
      dccGraph(id = 'graph', figure=fig),
      htmlPre(
        id='structure',
        style = list(border = 'thin lightgrey solid',
                     overflowY = 'scroll',
                     height = '275px')
      )
    )
  )
)
app$callback(
  output(id = 'structure', property='children'),
  params=list(input(id='graph', property='figure')),
  function(fig_json) {
    jfig <- plotly_json(fig, jsonedit = FALSE)
    return(jfig)
  })
#app$run_server()

Use app$run_server() to run the dash app.

Creating Figures

This section summarizes several ways to create new figures with the plotly.core graphing library.

Plotly Scatter Plot 

library(plotly.core)
data(iris)

fig <- go_figure()
for (sp in levels(iris$Species)) {
  fig <- fig |>
    add_scatter(
      data = iris[iris$Species == sp, ],
      x = ~Sepal.Width,
      y = ~Sepal.Length,
      mode = "markers",
      name = sp
    )
}
fig <- fig |>
  update_layout(
    title = "A Plotly Figure",
    legend = go_legend(title = go_legend_title(text = "species")),
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff"),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff")
  )
fig

Make Subplots

The make_subplots() function produces a figure that is preconfigured with a grid of subplots that traces can be added to.

library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(rows = 1, cols = 2) |>
  add_scatter(y = c(4, 2, 1), mode = "lines", row = 1, col = 1) |>
  add_bar(y = c(2, 1, 3), row = 1, col = 2) |>
  update_xaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_yaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6")
fig

Updating Figures

Regardless of how a figure was constructed, it can be updated by adding additional traces to it and modifying its properties.

Adding Traces

New traces can be added to a figure using add_trace() (with a graph object such as go_bar()) or the add_<type>() functions such as add_bar(). This allows you to start with an empty figure, and add traces to it sequentially.

library(plotly.core)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_trace(go_bar(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(1, 3, 2))) |>
  update_xaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_yaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6")
fig
library(plotly.core)
data(iris)

fig <- go_figure()
for (sp in levels(iris$Species)) {
  fig <- fig |>
    add_scatter(
      data = iris[iris$Species == sp, ],
      x = ~Sepal.Width,
      y = ~Sepal.Length,
      mode = "markers",
      name = sp
    )
}
fig <- fig |>
  update_layout(
    title = "Using The add_trace() method With A Plotly Figure",
    legend = go_legend(title = go_legend_title(text = "species")),
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff"),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff")
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    go_scatter(
      x = c(2, 4),
      y = c(4, 8),
      mode = "lines",
      line = go_scatter_line(color = "grey"),
      showlegend = FALSE
    )
  )
fig

Updating Figure Layouts

Figures support an update_layout() function that may be used to update multiple nested properties of a figure’s layout.

Here is an example of updating the font size of a figure’s title using update_layout().

library(plotly.core)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_bar(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(1, 3, 2)) |>
  update_layout(
    title = go_layout_title(
      text = "Using update_layout() With Plotly Figures",
      font = go_font(size = 17)
    ),
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6",
    xaxis = go_xaxis(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff"),
    yaxis = go_yaxis(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff")
  )
fig

Updating Traces

Figures support an update_traces() function that may be used to update multiple nested properties of one or more of a figure’s traces.

To show some examples, we will start with a figure that contains bar and scatter traces across two subplots.

library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(rows = 1, cols = 2) |>
  add_bar(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(2, 1, 3),
    name = "b",
    marker = go_bar_marker(color = "red"),
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(4, 2, 3.5),
    mode = "markers",
    name = "a",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(size = 20, color = "rgb(51, 204, 51)"),
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_bar(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(1, 3, 2),
    name = "c",
    marker = go_bar_marker(color = "#33cc33"),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(2, 3.5, 4),
    mode = "markers",
    name = "d",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(size = 20, color = "rgb(255, 0, 0)"),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  update_xaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_yaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6")
fig

Note that both scatter and bar traces have a marker.color property to control their coloring. Here is an example of using update_traces() to modify the color of all traces.

library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(rows = 1, cols = 2) |>
  add_bar(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(2, 1, 3),
    name = "b",
    marker = go_bar_marker(color = "red"),
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(4, 2, 3.5),
    mode = "markers",
    name = "a",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(size = 20, color = "rgb(51, 204, 51)"),
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_bar(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(1, 3, 2),
    name = "c",
    marker = go_bar_marker(color = "#33cc33"),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(2, 3.5, 4),
    mode = "markers",
    name = "d",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(size = 20, color = "rgb(255, 0, 0)"),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  update_xaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_yaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_traces(marker = go_bar_marker(color = "blue"))
fig

The update_traces() function supports a selector argument to control which traces should be updated. Only traces that match the selector (a trace type, trace indices, a named list of property values, or a function) will be updated. row and col restrict the update to the traces of one subplot. Here is an example of using a selector to only update the color of the bar traces.

library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(rows = 1, cols = 2) |>
  add_bar(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(2, 1, 3),
    name = "b",
    marker = go_bar_marker(color = "red"),
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(4, 2, 3.5),
    mode = "markers",
    name = "a",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(size = 20, color = "rgb(51, 204, 51)"),
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_bar(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(1, 3, 2),
    name = "c",
    marker = go_bar_marker(color = "#33cc33"),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(2, 3.5, 4),
    mode = "markers",
    name = "d",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(size = 20, color = "rgb(255, 0, 0)"),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  update_xaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_yaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_traces(marker = go_bar_marker(color = "blue"), selector = "bar")
fig

Overwrite Existing Properties When Using Update Methods

update_traces() and update_layout() merge the new values into existing nested properties. Use overwrite = TRUE to replace the prior value of existing properties with the provided value instead.

In the example below, the red color of markers is overwritten when updating marker with overwrite = TRUE.

library(plotly.core)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_bar(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(1, 3, 2), marker = go_bar_marker(color = "red")) |>
  update_xaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_yaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6")

update_traces(fig, marker = go_bar_marker(opacity = 0.4), overwrite = TRUE)

Updating Figure Axes

Figures support update_xaxes() and update_yaxes() functions that may be used to update multiple nested properties of one or more of a figure’s axes. Here is an example of using update_xaxes() to disable the vertical grid lines across all subplots in a figure.

library(plotly.core)
data(iris)

species <- levels(iris$Species)
fig <- make_subplots(
  rows = 1,
  cols = 3,
  shared_yaxes = TRUE,
  subplot_titles = paste0("species=", species)
)
for (i in seq_along(species)) {
  fig <- fig |>
    add_scatter(
      data = iris[iris$Species == species[[i]], ],
      x = ~Sepal.Width,
      y = ~Sepal.Length,
      mode = "markers",
      name = species[[i]],
      row = 1,
      col = i
    )
}
fig <- fig |>
  update_annotations(font = go_font(size = 10)) |>
  update_layout(
    title = "Updating x axis in a Plotly Figure",
    legend = go_legend(title = go_legend_title(text = "species")),
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_xaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, showgrid = FALSE)

fig

Other Update Methods

Figures created with the plotly.core graphing library also support:

  • update_layout_images() in order to update background layout images,
  • update_annotations() in order to update annotations,
  • and update_shapes() in order to update shapes.

Chaining Figure Operations

All of the figure update operations described above are functions that return the modified figure. This makes it possible to chain multiple figure modification operations together into a single expression with the pipe.

Here is an example of a chained expression that:

  • sets the title font size using layout.title.font.size,
  • disables vertical grid lines using update_xaxes(),
  • updates the size and color of the markers and bar using update_traces(),
  • and then displaying the figure.
library(plotly.core)

t <- go_font(size = 15)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_bar(x = c(0, 1, 2), y = c(2, 1, 3), name = "b", marker = go_bar_marker(color = "red")) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(4, 2, 3.5),
    mode = "markers",
    name = "a",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(size = 10, color = "rgb(51, 204, 51)")
  ) |>
  # updates the size and color of the markers and bar
  update_traces(marker = go_scatter_marker(size = 20, color = "blue"), selector = "scatter") |>
  update_traces(
    marker = go_bar_marker(
      color = "yellow",
      line = go_bar_marker_line(color = "rgb(8,48,107)", width = 1.5)
    ),
    selector = "bar"
  ) |>
  update_layout(
    title = go_layout_title(
      text = "Chaining Multiple Figure Operations With A Plotly Figure",
      # setting the title font size
      font = t
    ),
    plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6"
  ) |>
  # disables vertical grid lines
  update_xaxes(showgrid = FALSE, zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2) |>
  update_yaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff")
# displaying the figure
fig

Property Assignment

Trace and layout properties can be updated using property assignment syntax. Here is an example of setting the figure title using property assignment.

library(plotly.core)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_bar(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(1, 3, 2)) |>
  update_xaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_yaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6")
fig$layout$title <- go_layout_title(text = "Using Property Assignment Syntax With A Plotly Figure")

fig

And here is an example of updating the bar outline using property assignment.

library(plotly.core)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_bar(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(1, 3, 2)) |>
  update_xaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_yaxes(zerolinecolor = "#ffff", zerolinewidth = 2, gridcolor = "#ffff") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6")
fig$data[[1]]$marker$line$color <- "black"
fig$data[[1]]$marker$line$width <- 4

fig
